q: Where exactly does the paper's Eq. (9) obtain the index rule delta_{l - (-1)^{j'}, l'} vs. the symmetric reading delta_{l - (-1)^{j}, l'}? The former (as printed) makes u_beta non-Hermitian, contradicting the paper's own claim that u_beta is unitary AND Hermitian.
basis: Coding Eq. (9) literally from the pdftotext extraction of arXiv:1711.11336v3 gave a non-symmetric 5x5 matrix (dev ~1.0 in ||B - B^T||); switching to the symmetric reading j->j (not j->j') yielded ||B - B^T|| = 0 and ||B B^T - I|| < 5e-16 across the whole sweep. This is either a printed typo in the paper or a subtle mis-rendering by pdftotext of a hat/prime we couldn't see.
next_steps: Fetch the LaTeX source from arXiv (arXiv:1711.11336 source tarball), inspect Eq. (9) in the source, and either confirm the typo (submit erratum to author Renato Portugal <portugal@lncc.br>) or re-derive the printed form from the tessellation definition (Eq. 3-4) and check whether an alternative basis convention makes it self-consistent.

q: Is the small negative bias in the log-log slope of Q vs N (observed 0.665 vs theory 0.667) a genuine finite-size correction predictable from the sub-leading terms of t1 = pi*sqrt(r)/4 + O(r^{(k-2)/(2k)}) (Eq. 28), or an artifact of the integer-rounding of r, t1, t2 in our enumeration?
basis: Our sweep uses N in [15, 3000] and gets slope 0.6646; theory is 0.6667. The gap is ~0.003 in slope, which is real but small. r_optimal, t1_optimal, t2_optimal are all rounded to nearest integer, which introduces a staircase that biases finite-N fits.
next_steps: Repeat the sweep with (i) much larger N (up to N=1e5 -- still trivial in the (2k+1)-dim reduction), and (ii) fractional t1/t2 emulated by evolving u^theta = expm(theta * log(u)) for theta ~ pi*sqrt(r)/(2*sqrt(k)) exactly. Compare fitted exponents in each case. If integer-rounding is the cause, the fractional version should give slope ~ 0.6667.

q: At N=15 and N=30 we see a noticeable dip in p_succ (0.64 and 0.72) below neighbors at N=9, 12, 20. The paper's asymptotic bound is silent on non-monotone pre-asymptotic behavior. Is this dip explained by t1-rounding falling short of the true amplitude-amplification maximum, or by an interference resonance with a subleading eigenvalue of u^{t2} R?
basis: Observed in Table 1 of the report: p_succ(N=9)=0.80, p_succ(N=12)=0.79, p_succ(N=15)=0.64 (dip), p_succ(N=20)=0.93, p_succ(N=30)=0.72 (dip). p_max at the argmax step doesn't fully recover it either -- these are genuine pre-asymptotic troughs.
next_steps: Diagonalize u^{t2} R at each N in [10, 50], track the 5 eigenvalues on the unit circle, and correlate the dips with near-degeneracies. Also try t1 = floor and t1 = ceil (not just round) and see which local troughs vanish.

q: The improved constant c_2 = pi/(2*sqrt(k)) of this paper is claimed to push asymptotic p_succ from Ambainis' 75% to 100%. In our finite-N sweep, even at N=3000 we sit at p_succ = 0.975. How large must N be before observed p_succ crosses 0.99? This matters for the amplitude-amplification overhead in downstream applications (Grover-boosted triangle finding, quantum attacks on iterated ciphers, etc.).
basis: Table 1 shows 1 - p_succ shrinking from 0.44 (N=6) to 0.025 (N=3000), and the ratio (1-p_succ)/r^{-1/k} is O(1) but not visibly constant. Extrapolating naively, N ~ 30000 would put us at 1 - p_succ ~ 0.010.
next_steps: Run the reduced-subspace sim at a log-spaced grid up to N ~ 3e5 (still numpy-only, milliseconds per point). Fit 1-p_succ = A * r^{-1/k} + B * r^{-2/k} + ..., report A, B, and the crossover N for p_succ = 0.99, 0.999, 1 - 1e-6.

q: Does the same (2k+1)-dimensional reduction work verbatim for k=3 (giving Q ~ N^{3/4} per Ambainis) using our same u_alpha, u_beta formulas? Belovs (2012) already beats this for k>=3 using learning graphs, but numerically confirming the k=3 baseline in the same reduced formalism would establish the reduction as a reusable tool for larger k.
basis: This replication only tested k=2 because that is the classic element-distinctness case and the paper's title. Our build_u_alpha, build_u_beta, build_R, build_psi0, r_optimal, t1_optimal, t2_optimal all take k as a parameter and should work at k=3 with only a change in the calling code (7x7 matrices instead of 5x5).
next_steps: Extend the sweep to k=3 and k=4, verify slopes of log Q vs log N match k/(k+1) = 0.75 and 0.80. Then measure the log-log ratio between the Portugal query count and the Belovs learning-graph query count at N = 100, 1000, 10000 to quantify the k>=3 improvement gap numerically.
